Maladaptive Strategies.value: I detach myself from the memories
I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts
Being alone in a room or building

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

vignette: Thomas had come to understand that the violence began not with a shout, but with the slow tightening of his former male partner’s grip around his wrists in the narrow hallway. He was fifty-four now, living with his current partner in a quiet suburban home, but the past still intrudes with the force of a physical blow. When the event surfaces, it does not arrive as a narrative he can piece together; he finds it incredibly difficult to recall deliberately, his mind simply refusing to yield the timeline. Instead, the experience returns as a series of stark, unblinking photographs locked behind his eyes. The moment these images break through, a vivid taste of copper and damp wool floods his mouth, visceral and undeniable. The sheer helplessness of those early months dictated how Thomas survived the years that followed. The moment he perceived a threat to his autonomy, or found himself cornered by another man, his body seized on the old panic. That sudden fear of losing control, compounded by the dread of sleeping alone or being alone with men, drove him to manufacture constant company. He filled his evenings with loud dinners, crowded community meetings, and back-to-back social calls, knowing that if he ever fell quiet, the vulnerability would overwhelm him. He avoided being alone in a room or building with the precision of a man who knows exactly which floorboards crack, and this relentless strategy was the direct, automatic response to his triggers. Working as a civil servant in a municipal records archive, Thomas’s environment became a quiet minefield. The heavy oak doors, the deep hum of the ventilation, or the sudden footfalls of a male colleague in the corridor could instantly fracture his composure. The mere presence of these cues immediately pulled the photographic memories forward, stripping away his defenses and flooding his senses with that sharp, metallic taste. He was certain that if he stopped moving, the past would catch him, so the environmental triggers did not merely remind him of the event; they actively dragged the fragmented, taste-laden images into his conscious awareness. Yet the memories themselves were not passive ghosts; they were active instigators. Every time a photographic image flashed in his mind, unbidden and relentless, it recalibrated his nervous system, turning a benign interaction into a perceived threat. The sudden sight of a man’s hand reaching across a desk, the echo of a heavy door clicking shut, or the silence of his own bedroom at night would ignite instantly, transforming a neutral moment into a crisis of suffocation. The memories did not just return; they forged new triggers out of ordinary life. His attempts to outrun the past only deepened the wound. His strategy of detaching himself from the memories was meant to act as a buffer, yet the constant socialising and avoidance of being alone in a room or building eventually depleted his cognitive reserves. When the noise finally faded, the mental exhaustion pulled down the barriers he had built, allowing the photographic recall to surface unguarded. At the same time, this very avoidance created a feedback loop of hypervigilance; his nervous system never learned to process ordinary safety, so the constant need to stay surrounded by people left him perpetually braced for impact. His strategies had not insulated him; they had sensitised him, ensuring that even a dropped file folder could reignite the very triggers he had tried so hard to escape. What finally brought Thomas to seek help was not the memories themselves, but the way his avoidance had eroded his relationship and his work. He was terrified of being evaluated as broken, yet he desperately hoped for a way to sleep through the night without checking the locks three times. He wanted the photographs to stop arriving when he needed to file a report, and for the taste of that hallway to fade into something he could remember without his heart hammering against his ribs. He was ready, finally, to stop running and learn how to stay.
